title: Illegal vs Unwanted States
author: Hillel Wayne
note: A useful distinction for system design: some states must never occur, while others need to be visible and eventually resolved. It connects everyday product decisions to safety and liveness without treating every awkward intermediate state as a modeling mistake.

title: CI at Scale: Lean, Green, and Fast
author: Dhruva Juloori, Zhongpeng Lin, Matthew Williams, Eddy Shin, Sonal Mahajan
note: Worth reading for its view of CI scheduling as a decision problem: prioritize the set of build results needed to safely merge a change, rather than just the most likely path. The SubmitQueue case makes the trade-off between speculative work, latency, and correctness concrete.

title: Agent Observability Needs Feedback to Power Learning
author: Harrison Chase
note: A clear account of why traces need quality signals. Connecting user feedback and evaluations to runs turns observability into a way to improve the model, harness, and context—useful when designing an agent platform beyond logs and dashboards.

title: The software industry: annealing, but wrong
author: apenwarr
note: A useful challenge to treating small PRs as a universal rule. As AI makes large changes cheaper to generate, the harder engineering problem becomes reviewing, validating, and rejecting experiments quickly enough to let good designs emerge.

title: Formal methods and the future of programming
author: Yaron Minsky
note: Explains why agentic coding changes the economics of formal methods: proof tools can become easier to use just as generated code makes verification more urgent. Especially relevant to treating specifications and proofs as feedback infrastructure for coding agents.

title: Specula: Scaling formal specifications for autonomous model checking of system code
author: Murat Demirbas
note: A valuable account of both the power and the limits of automated formal methods. The trace, model-checking, and reproduction loops are worth studying, while the critique keeps a crucial distinction in view: finding reproducible bugs does not establish that inferred specifications capture the intended behavior.
